transcript: The young prodigy captures the knight. By far the best move in the position. After all, this is Dennis Lazavvich from Bellarus, a 19-year-old Prodigy Grandmaster. But his opponent, Eddis Guell, is no less than another Prodigy and Grandmaster. And he takes back with the bishop, now bringing it to a very active diagonal. Dennis brings a rook to the H file, now piling up a lot of pressure around this king. And here Edis tries to be tricky with knight to E5. Now this move is attacking the queen and the bishop at the same time. The idea is very clever actually. If we take this knight, now the rook is going to sacrifice itself on C1. A double sacrifice. And after white takes with the knight, black is going to play this skewer here, attacking the rook behind the king. And now if you capture like this, you're going to lose the knight. And if you take with the king, queen to F2 is going to lead to a checkmating attack. But Dennis, being the incredible player that he is, sees all of this and instead plays the incredible and majestic bishop to [music] B2. A brilliant move that sacrifices the queen. But of course, you cannot take the queen because otherwise rook to H8 check. Another sacrifice is going to lead to a checkmate in just two moves. And you might think, is this it? Is this the most beautiful move of the year? Well, not exactly. You see, I have a confession to make. I have not been exactly genuine with you. Because you see, bishop to B2 is actually Yes. A blunder. A blunder? How? We saw that you cannot take the queen because of the checkmate, right? How can this possibly be a blunder? Well, in this position, Eddie Guell played the best move of 2025. The incredible, the majestic, the supreme queen to F2 check. A move that looks like the most outrageous blunder you could possibly think of, throwing the queen directly into the white position. This move doesn't even capture anything. How can this possibly be a good move, but hear me while I say this, this is not only a good move, this is the only move in the position that doesn't lose the game. Which means that this move had to be foreseen when Edis decided to play knight to E5. So, okay, what's the point? Well, first of all, the queen has to be taken. If you take with the king, this is pretty simple. I'm now going to capture the queen with a check, meaning that at the end of the day, black is going to win a full piece. And if you take with the rook, well, now I'm still going to capture like this. Now, I'm attacking the rook and the undefended bishop. So, the game continued with bishop takes G7, knight takes F2, and now this move also attacks the other rook. So, you have to do something about that. Meaning that white took the knight, black took the bishop. So ultimately all of this was done so that Edis could end up with a rook for a knight which at this level is going to be enough for a grandmaster to win the game.
